CUPMem handles older memories at write time via state adjudication rather than query-time reconciliation. An LLM adjudicator assigns each candidate old state one of KEEP, STALE, REPLACE, or UNKNOWN [2605.06527#s15.p1]. Stale states are archived rather than deleted, and unsafe slots without a settled replacement are marked UNKNOWN_CURRENT [2605.06527#s63.p10]. A topology-triggered search expands invalidation to structurally affected state regions, so propagated conflicts are retired before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. At readout, only authorized state is consumed: active items ground answers, stale items serve as historical context, and unresolved slots block unsafe old defaults [2605.06527#s15.p1]. This raises overall accuracy from 8.7% to 68.0% under the same GPT-4o-mini backbone [2605.06527#s15.p1].

Full-tree search outperforms retrieval restricted to specific layers [2401.18059#s17.p4].

respuesta: The paper is "From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization" (GraphRAG, arXiv 2404.16130). It targets global questions aimed at an entire corpus, such as "What are the main themes in the dataset?" [2404.16130#s1.p1][2404.16130#s2.p1]. An LLM derives an entity knowledge graph and then pregenerates community summaries for groups of closely related entities [2404.16130#s1.p1]; each community summary yields a partial response that is map-reduced into a final answer [2404.16130#s1.p1][2404.16130#s15.p3].

"Don't Do RAG: When Cache-Augmented Generation is All You Need for Knowledge Tasks" (Huang et al., arXiv 2412.15605) proposes cache-augmented generation: it preloads all relevant documents into a long-context LLM and precomputes the key-value (KV) cache encapsulating the model's inference state, then answers queries from that cache with no retrieval step [2412.15605#s2.p3][2412.15605#s3.p2]. FactConsolidation is introduced in the paper with arXiv id 2507.05257 (the selective-forgetting / MemoryAgentBench work). It is built from MQUAKE counterfactual edit pairs concatenated into 6K, 32K, 64K, and 262K-token contexts, with single-hop and multi-hop question variants [2507.05257#s14.p1].

respuesta: FactConsolidation is introduced in the paper "Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions" (arXiv 2507.05257), which presents the MemoryAgentBench benchmark; FactConsolidation-SH and -MH are its selective-forgetting datasets, built from MQUAKE counterfactual edit pairs with newer facts placed after older ones [2507.05257#s8.p4][2507.05257#s14.p1].

MemoryAgentBench tests four competencies: Accurate Retrieval (AR), Test-Time Learning (TTL), Long-Range Understanding (LRU), and Selective Forgetting (SF) [2507.05257#s2.p2]. AR is extracting the correct snippet for a query (one-hop or multi-hop); TTL is acquiring new behaviors/skills during deployment without additional training; LRU is integrating information across extended contexts (≥100k tokens) for global understanding; SF is revising, overwriting, or removing stored information when faced with contradictory evidence [2507.05257#s2.p2].

The paper is A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents (arXiv 2502.12110). It follows the Zettelkasten method — the note-taking system of German sociologist Niklas Luhmann — using atomic notes, flexible linking, and continuous evolution of the knowledge network [2502.12110#s6.p1]. Each note stores content, timestamp, LLM-generated keywords, tags, and context, plus an embedding and a set of linked memories [2502.12110#s7.p2][2502.12110#s7.p3]; links are generated by embedding-based top-k candidate filtering followed by LLM judgment [2502.12110#s8.p2][2502.12110#s8.p6].

pasos.argumento: agent notes linked Zettelkasten Luhmann note-taking

respuesta: The paper is A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents (arXiv 2502.12110). It organizes an agent's memory as atomic notes linked to each other, following the Zettelkasten method — the note-taking system of German sociologist Niklas Luhmann [2502.12110#s6.p1]. New notes are linked via embedding-filtered LLM link generation [2502.12110#s8.p2][2502.12110#s8.p6].

LightMem (arXiv 2510.18866) is the paper. It is inspired by the Atkinson–Shiffrin model of human memory and organizes memory into three stages—sensory memory, short-term memory (STM), and long-term memory (LTM)—to cut token consumption and API calls while improving QA accuracy [2510.18866#s1.p1][2510.18866#s6.p1]. Its Light1 sensory compression, Light2 topic-aware STM buffer, and Light3 sleep-time LTM update reduce cost by up to 38× tokens and 30× API calls [2510.18866#s13.p2].

pasos.argumento: memory system tokens sleep stages short-term long-term storage

respuesta: LightMem (arXiv 2510.18866) is the paper: it is inspired by the Atkinson–Shiffrin model of human memory and organizes memory into three stages — sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory — with a sleep-time offline long-term update, cutting token consumption and API calls [2510.18866#s1.p1][2510.18866#s6.p1]. Its sensory pre-compression, topic-aware short-term buffer, and offline long-term store reduce tokens by up to 38× (combined) or 105.9× counting only online cost [2510.18866#s13.p2][2510.18866#s13.p3].

HaluMem is the benchmark: it is the first operation-level hallucination evaluation benchmark for memory systems, scoring extraction, updating, and QA stages with stage-specific gold standards [2511.03506#s1.p1][2511.03506#s6.p8]. It measures fabricated extraction via False Memory Resistance (fraction of distractors ignored) [2511.03506#s12.p2], and hallucination rates for updating and QA [2511.03506#s14.p6][2511.03506#s15.p5].

pasos.argumento: memory system hallucination false facts benchmark

respuesta: HaluMem is the benchmark: it is an operation-level hallucination evaluation benchmark for memory systems that scores memory extraction, memory updating, and memory question answering separately, so fabricated facts can be localized to the stage where they arise [2511.03506#s1.p1][2511.03506#s5.p6]. Its metrics include hallucination rates for updating and QA, plus False Memory Resistance for extraction [2511.03506#s12.p2][2511.03506#s14.p6][2511.03506#s15.p5].

LongMemEval tests five long-term memory abilities: (1) information extraction — recalling details stated by the user or assistant [2410.10813#s8.p2]; (2) multi-session reasoning — aggregating and comparing information across sessions [2410.10813#s8.p2]; (3) knowledge updates — tracking changes in user information over time [2410.10813#s8.p2]; (4) temporal reasoning — using explicit time mentions and timestamp metadata [2410.10813#s8.p2]; and (5) abstention — answering "I don't know" for unmentioned information [2410.10813#s8.p2]. These are operationalized by seven question types plus 30 false-premise abstention questions [2410.10813#s8.p3].

pasos.argumento: LongMemEval benchmark abilities

respuesta: LongMemEval tests five core long-term memory abilities: information extraction (recall specific details from extensive histories, including those stated by the assistant) [2410.10813#s8.p2], multi-session reasoning (synthesize information across sessions for aggregation and comparison) [2410.10813#s8.p2], knowledge updates (recognize changes in user information over time) [2410.10813#s8.p2], temporal reasoning (use explicit time mentions and timestamp metadata) [2410.10813#s8.p2], and abstention (answer "I don't know" for unmentioned information) [2410.10813#s8.p2]. These are operationalized by seven question types plus 30 false-premise abstention questions [2410.10813#s8.p3].
